greeting.text: The hut window is shuttered. Coyle has taken the ledgers from the rack and stacked them. "Four wardens and an overseer," she says, still writing. "I've entered it as an incident. Incidents go in the day book, and the book goes downriver on the fifth." She blots the page. "I'm not frightened of you. This works needs me more than it needed Rourke. He knew it too."

"Dale's account," Coyle says, already taking it from the rack. She fetches it twice a week for someone. "Here's his indenture. Here's the reckoning of days. They're two sheets." She aligns them on the desk. "He was given the first. He's never asked for the second. I'd give it to him. Nobody's asked."

The hut is warm, dry, and better lit than anywhere else down here. Its window faces the muster line, placed just so. Coyle looks up from the water clock. "You've been on my floor an hour and forty minutes without a peg," she says. "That's not an accusation. It's a column I can't fill."

choices.label: I'm not going in your book.
Then I'll go back up the stair.

greeting.text: "You've walked the muster floor, the canteen, four of the six faces and the wet way," Coyle says. "I know because there's a boy on each, paid to know." She takes quiet pride in her system. "What are you counting? Save yourself the walk. I count everything here, and better than you do."

choices.label: Two hundred people and nobody guarding the door.

greeting.text: "I'm to send word if you come through the yard," Coyle says before you can speak. "There's a form, with a space for the hour." She slides it face down under the ledger. She hasn't torn it up, and doesn't pretend otherwise. "Word goes with the tallies at shift's end. That's when it goes." She turns the water clock a quarter and sets it down. "You have until then."

Coyle has a sheet out that isn't a time sheet. "You're on this one," she says, without turning it round. "It came up on the wages cart with the pegs. It isn't signed or marked with a purpose. I put it in the box with the signed ones because there's nowhere else for it." She dates the corner. "I write down what I see. I've written when you came, and how long you stayed, as I do for a hundred and four others. I won't make an exception for you."

"One hundred and four," Coyle says without looking up. She knew your peg by the sound of your boots. "Bring the lamp back at shift's end. If you break the gauze, tell me. A man who hides a broken gauze kills eleven people and himself."

choices.label: What's at the bottom of it all?

greeting.text: Coyle glances up, notes the time and writes it on the second sheet. "You're on my other list," she says. "You're the only name that keeps coming back. I found that interesting enough to mention to nobody."

choices.label: What's at the bottom of it all?

greeting.text: "You went up the stair, and now you're back down. I wrote down both, and I'll write this down too." Coyle dips her pen. "I'm not making a point. I write down everything that happens on this floor."

choices.label: Give me a peg after all.

greeting.text: "You've seen all of it now," Coyle says. "Muster, canteen, six faces, the wet way and the office ladder." She turns a peg on the board without looking at you. "There's nothing else to see. People never believe that, so they keep coming back down."

choices.label: What's at the bottom of it all?

greeting.text: "You were on the muster floor for eleven minutes on the ninth, then left," Coyle says. "Now here you are again." She isn't gloating; she's stating a fact. "People come back. In three years, four went up and didn't return. Two were dead within the year, from ordinary things."

choices.label: What's at the bottom of it all?

greeting.text: "One hundred and four," Coyle says, without looking up, because she knew which peg came through the door by the sound of the boots. "Lamp back at the end of shift. If you break the gauze you say so; a man who hides a broken gauze kills eleven people and himself."

choices.label: What's at the bottom of it all?

greeting.text: A plank hut, warm and dry, with a window, a water clock, a bell rope, a rack of tallies and four ledgers. The woman inside writes until she finishes the line. "Coyle," she says. "Timekeeper. Peg number."

choices.label: I haven't got a peg number.

then_we_shall_see.text: Coyle sets down her pen and gives you her full attention. "Then you're one of four things: new, lost, a thief, or from downriver. I have a form for three." She waits. She won't call anyone; she'll wait.

interjections.text: Sera: "She hasn't asked who we are. She asked which box we go in. Those are different questions, and the second is harder to lie about."

choices.label: Give her a name and take a peg.

what_this_is.text: "The works," Coyle says. "Six faces, two hundred and eleven on the books, a hundred and ninety working today. Three shifts, two bells, one canteen. Timber comes down the stair; spoil goes up, and both are counted." She gestures toward the board without turning. "That's what it is. There's no second answer underneath, though people are always disappointed by that."

the_board.text: She turns the ledger so you can see it, the first person down here to do so. Two hundred and eleven names, each with a peg number, and a column of hours going back three years without a gap. "That's the works," she says. "Not the stone. This. Anyone can dig a hole. Keeping two hundred people in one for three years without a riot is the trade."

interjections.text: Ilse: "Three years. You've been under my warren for three years." Coyle, mildly: "Two years and nine months. Don't say three in front of Rourke; he's sensitive about the first winter."

choices.label: I'd rather not be in anybody's book.
Who keeps the book above yours?

peg_one_oh_four.text: "One hundred and four," she says, writing it down. She doesn't ask for another name. She hands you a caged lamp and a tally with the number scratched on it, then turns a peg on the board. Now you're a fact about this place, and nobody down here will look at you again while it's turned.

interjections.text: Kessa: "That's it? That's the security?" Coyle: "That's the security. It's held for three years. Your friend's warden fence hasn't."

the_other_sheet.text: "Then you go on the other sheet," Coyle says. She fetches another and writes in the same hand, at the same speed. "People on the works who aren't on the books. It's a short list. I've kept it since the first winter, and nobody's asked to see it." She blots the page. "I'm not annoyed. There's a column for everything, and it's better if each thing is in the right one."

she_writes_that_too.text: She records the time you left, as she does for everyone, then returns to the water clock. Halfway up the stair, you realise she never asked your business. She's never needed to know anyone's business.

no_door_to_guard.text: "There's no door," Coyle agrees. "A door needs a man, a man needs pay, and a man can be got round. A peg can't. If you're not on the board, you're not fed, lit, paid, or carried out if the roof comes down." She dips her pen. "Anyone here could walk up the stair this afternoon. Not one will, and I haven't spent a penny stopping them."

interjections.text: Aldric: "You've made a prison out of a ledger." Coyle, evenly: "I made a payroll, brother. You called it a prison."
Sera has gone pale. "I could have written this," she says. "That's what I keep thinking. I could have written every page."

choices.label: What is at the bottom of it?

not_my_column.text: "Not my column," Coyle says. "I track hours, heads, timber, oil, spoil and the bell. Where the spoil comes from is in Rourke's book; what it's for is in downriver's. I've never opened either, and I'd be poor at it." She returns to the clock. "Everyone here knows their own column. That isn't stupidity. It's how a thing this size gets done."

rourke.text: "Overseer. Up the ladder, above the headings, with the shutter open. That's where he belongs, and where he likes to be." She pauses. "He came up through the faces; he'll tell you in four minutes. He keeps the working paper. Ask him what they're cutting, or why the six faces point where they do. That's his rack, not mine."

the_second_sheet.text: It's the reckoning of days, and it's correct. None of it favours Dale: days lost to water, days lost to a bad face, lamp and bread charged against wages, bread at a halfpenny over. The cow's carriage is entered twice, once as keep. Every line is honest. The sum is that Corrin Dale signed for three years and has bought himself about eight months.

interjections.text: Kessa: "There's no cheating here." Coyle: "None. I wouldn't keep a crooked book. It would be worse for me, and there's no need."

choices.label: Copy it. He should see it.

she_lets_you.text: She turns the sheet round, finds you a pen, and looks away while you copy it. At the end, she blots it out of habit. "Tell him it's not a trick," she says. "That's what they never believe, and the only thing that's kept me awake. There's no trick. It's just the arithmetic, done properly by someone paid to do it properly."

by_the_fifteenth.text: "By the fifteenth," Coyle says. "There's a man at Greyhythe who does nothing else. The works will lose four days, and those days come off everyone's reckoning. I'll have to explain that a hundred and ninety times."

the_end_of_the_shift.text: "Because a hundred and ninety people work under me, and every one knows exactly what I write about them," Coyle says. "That's the arrangement. It's what makes the day book worth anything, and I won't spend that trust on you." She glances at the shuttered window, then at the clock. "The bell rings at shift's end. I won't ring it early or late."
